TRADE SECRET INJUNCTIVE RELIEF STANDARDS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS TRADE SECRET INJUNCTIVE RELIEF STANDARDS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the statutory standards governing injunctions in trade secret misappropriation cases under California Civil Code section 3426.2, part of the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA), and under the parallel federal injunctive-relief provision of the Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(3)(A). It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning Acme, Inc.'s trade secret, described as follows: Acme's proprietary customer-pricing algorithm and associated source code, in a situation involving Beta Corp. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what these statutes say about the injunction remedy specifically -- when a court may enjoin actual or threatened misappropriation, when such an injunction must be terminated or may be continued, when a court may substitute a reasonable royalty for an injunction, and when a court may compel affirmative acts to protect a trade secret. It does not itself determine whether an injunction would be granted, denied, modified, or terminated in any specific case, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and is meant as a companion to, this project's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter document: that document addresses the definition of misappropriation and the damages and attorney's-fee remedies available for it, while this one addresses a separate question -- the standards governing the injunctive relief remedy specifically.

CALIFORNIA: ENJOINING ACTUAL OR THREATENED MISAPPROPRIATION, AND WHEN AN INJUNCTION MUST END
Under California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act, actual or threatened misappropriation of a trade secret may be enjoined -- meaning an injunction is available not only after misappropriation has occurred, but also against misappropriation that is merely threatened. The statute also sets a rule for when such an injunction must end: upon application to the court, an injunction must be terminated once the trade secret has ceased to exist. But the statute allows an exception to immediate termination -- the injunction may instead be continued for an additional period of time where doing so is needed to eliminate a commercial advantage that would otherwise still be derived from the earlier misappropriation, even after the trade secret itself no longer exists as a trade secret.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Actual or threatened misappropriation may be enjoined. Upon application to the court, an injunction shall be terminated when the trade secret has ceased to exist, but the injunction may be continued for an additional period of time in order to eliminate commercial advantage that otherwise would be derived from the misappropriation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.2(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, injunctive relief -- enjoining misappropriation and termination of injunctions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.2.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of CUTSA's own stated standard for enjoining misappropriation and for terminating or continuing that injunction -- not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that an injunction would be granted, denied, terminated, or continued on any specific set of facts. This clause quotes subdivision (a) of Cal. Civ. Code section 3426.2; companion clauses in this document quote subdivisions (b) and (c) of that same section -- all three are subdivisions of one statutory section, not independent sources of each other, and are disclosed as such throughout this document. The statute does not itself define what showing a plaintiff must make to obtain a preliminary injunction (for example, likelihood of success or irreparable harm) -- those procedural standards come from other law, including the general California statute governing preliminary injunctions and case law construing it, neither of which is addressed here. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause was attempted but returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) before any case could be retrieved, so no case law on how California courts apply this standard -- including how courts treat a merely "threatened" misappropriation -- is included in this document; only the statutory text is quoted. The full text of section 3426.2 was retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov -- the official California Legislative Information website -- as two separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical text for the whole section.

CALIFORNIA: REASONABLE ROYALTY IN PLACE OF AN INJUNCTION
California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act does not treat an injunction as the only, or an automatic, remedy once misappropriation is shown. Where a court determines that it would be unreasonable to prohibit a defendant's future use of the trade secret, the statute allows the court instead to condition that future use upon payment of a reasonable royalty, running for no longer than the period during which the use could otherwise have been prohibited by injunction. This royalty-in-lieu-of-injunction mechanism is a distinct statutory option from the reasonable-royalty damages measure available under a separate provision of the same act.

This clause quotes subdivision (b) of Cal. Civ. The statute does not define "reasonable royalty" or specify a method for calculating one in this injunction-substitute context; this clause does not address how a court would calculate such a royalty. CALIFORNIA: COURT-ORDERED AFFIRMATIVE ACTS TO PROTECT A TRADE SECRET
Beyond prohibiting future misappropriation, California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act allows a court, in appropriate circumstances, to go further and affirmatively compel acts to protect a trade secret by court order. The statute does not itemize which specific acts a court may order; it states only that such affirmative acts may be compelled where circumstances make that appropriate, leaving the specific content of any such order to the court's judgment on the facts before it.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.2(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, injunctive relief -- compelled affirmative acts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.2.)

This clause quotes subdivision (c) of Cal. Civ. FEDERAL DTSA: ENJOINING ACTUAL OR THREATENED MISAPPROPRIATION
The federal Defend Trade Secrets Act contains its own injunctive-relief provision, structured similarly to California's but written and codified separately. In a civil action under the DTSA, a court may grant an injunction to prevent any actual or threatened misappropriation, on terms the court deems reasonable. As with California's statute, the DTSA's injunction authority reaches threatened misappropriation, not only misappropriation that has already occurred -- but the DTSA's grant of injunctive authority is also expressly made subject to limits set out elsewhere in the same subparagraph, addressed in a companion clause of this document, that do not appear in the California statute's text.

FEDERAL DTSA: EXPRESS LIMITS PROTECTING EMPLOYMENT MOBILITY AND STATE LAW
The DTSA's injunction authority to prevent actual or threatened misappropriation is expressly qualified by two limits that California's own trade secret injunction statute does not separately state in its own text. First, an injunction under the DTSA may not prevent a person from entering into an employment relationship; any conditions placed on such employment must be based on evidence of threatened misappropriation, not merely on the information the person knows. Second, a DTSA injunction may not otherwise conflict with an applicable state law prohibiting restraints on the practice of a lawful profession, trade, or business. Together, these limits mean a federal DTSA injunction cannot be used simply to bar someone from taking a new job based on the trade secrets they carry in their head, and cannot override a state's own restrictions on noncompete-style restraints.

FEDERAL DTSA: COURT-ORDERED AFFIRMATIVE ACTIONS TO PROTECT A TRADE SECRET
Paralleling California's statute, the DTSA also allows a court, if the court determines it appropriate, to require affirmative actions be taken to protect the trade secret. As with the California provision, the DTSA text does not enumerate which specific actions qualify, leaving that determination to the court on the facts of the case.

FEDERAL DTSA: REASONABLE ROYALTY IN EXCEPTIONAL CIRCUMSTANCES
The DTSA also contains its own royalty-in-lieu-of-injunction mechanism, narrower in its stated trigger than California's parallel provision. Where exceptional circumstances render an injunction inequitable, a court may instead condition future use of the trade secret upon payment of a reasonable royalty, for no longer than the period during which that use could otherwise have been prohibited. California's parallel provision is triggered by a court's determination that prohibiting future use would be "unreasonable," while the DTSA's text instead requires "exceptional circumstances" that render an injunction "inequitable" -- the two statutes use different trigger language for a similar remedy, and this document does not resolve whether that difference in wording produces a different practical standard.

California's parallel provision is triggered by a court's determination that prohibiting future use would be "unreasonable," while the DTSA's text instead requires "exceptional circumstances" that render an injunction "inequitable" -- the two statutes use different trigger language for a similar remedy, and this document does not resolve whether that difference in wording produces a different practical standard.

expectedJSON.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the DTSA's own stated standard for substituting a reasonable royalty for an injunction -- not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any court would find "exceptional circumstances" or order any particular royalty on any specific set of facts. This clause quotes 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(iii); companion clauses in this document quote (i), (i)(I)-(II), and (ii) of the same subparagraph -- all from the same statutory subparagraph, not independent sources of each other. The observation that the DTSA's "exceptional circumstances"/"inequitable" trigger differs in wording from California's "unreasonable" trigger is this document's own textual comparison of the two statutes, not a holding from any court; no case law addressing whether the two standards function differently in practice was checked (a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error, HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted, before any case could be retrieved).
